Sita Questions Rama's Vow

Stories from the Ramayana

Sita Questions Rama's Vow

Is Killing Without Enmity Still Dharma?

Everyday telling — Aranya Kanda, sargas 9–10

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read aloud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, the way you would sit with everyone at home and tell them a tale.

There is no battle in this book — there is a conversation. Between a husband and a wife, walking along a forest path. So read it even more slowly — as if two people were really talking.

The yellow boxes are where the characters speak in their own words. Change your voice a little as you read them — Sita soft and slow, Rama calm and grave.

(Cues in purple) tell you when to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

At the end of every section, a green box — Pause and Think. Stop there. Ask the questions. Let the listeners speak. The questions in this book are a little hard — they are for older listeners too.

The main story of this book comes from Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda, sargas 9–10. In the book before this one, Rama gave the sages his promise of protection — and that promise is the root of this story. Anything else you might want to know is given separately at the end, under Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Rama — the young prince of Ayodhya. Tall, calm, kind. Warm dark-brown skin, black hair tied back, simple gold jewellery, a bow in his hand. He has already promised the sages of the forest that he will protect them.

Sita — Rama's wife, princess of Mithila. Gentle oval face, large dark eyes, warm fair wheat-gold skin, long black hair centre-parted, a single long braid with small white jasmine flowers. Small gold jhumka earrings, a thin gold nose-ring on the left nostril, gold bangles, a simple gold necklace. In the forest a simple muted green-beige saree, no crown.

Lakshmana — Rama's younger brother. Like Rama, but a little younger and lighter in complexion. A bow in his hand, a simple green-beige forest dress. In this story Sita asks Rama to take counsel with Lakshmana too.

The sages of the Dandaka forest — the ascetics who live in the forest and are tormented by the rakshasas. They asked Rama for protection — and Rama gave his word.

The ascetic of the sword story — a holy sage of long ago, whose tale Sita tells Rama. He lived alone in the forest, in deep tapas (austerity).

Indra — king of the gods, who in that old tale comes in the guise of a warrior.

1 · Leaving Sutikshna · · LEAVING SUTIKSHNA

Taking leave of the sage Sutikshna's hermitage, the three set out again on the forest path — Rama ahead, Sita in the middle, Lakshmana behind, bow in hand.

The Dandaka forest spread all around them — tall trees, deep shade, and rivers flowing here and there. Birds were singing, and the air smelled of flowers.

But there was no peace in Sita's heart. For some days now, one thought had been turning round and round in her mind — and today, walking along the path, she gently wished to speak it to Rama.

Sita first looked at Rama — he was smiling, as if to say, "Speak, Sita, say whatever you have to say." Then Sita began to speak in a soft voice — as slow as the whisper of the wind.

Sita said: "Rama, I wish to say one thing to you — with love, and with respect. I have not sat down to teach you dharma — you are the very form of dharma. But my heart is full of worry, so I am speaking."

(Pause here — read slowly. Sita is speaking fearfully, but with love.)

Rama stopped. He looked at Sita — and began to listen. Lakshmana too stopped behind them.

Pause and think — Before speaking, Sita said — I have not come to teach you dharma. Is it good, when speaking to someone great, to first say — I am not teaching you, I am only telling you my worry? And does love give us the right to ask even hard questions of the one we love?

2 · Three Evils Born of Desire · · THREE EVILS BORN OF DESIRE

Sita said — "Rama, in this world three evils are born of desire."

"The first evil is — speaking falsehood. When desire wakes in the heart, lies come from the mouth."

"The second evil is — coveting another man's wife. It is a greater evil than the first."

"And the third evil is — enmity without cause. Hurting a person who has never done us any harm. This is the worst of the three."

Sita said: "Rama, it is this third evil that frightens me. You have promised the dwellers of the Dandaka forest that you will kill the rakshasas in battle. But those rakshasas have done you no harm. Will your bow itself become the cause of our sorrow?"

Sita went on — "Just as fire fed with wood bursts into flame, so the warrior spirit of a kshatriya flares up when a bow comes into his hand. I am afraid — that the moment you see a rakshasa, the urge to kill him will rise in you."

(Keep your voice low here — this is Sita's deepest fear.)

Pause and think — Sita counted three evils — falsehood, coveting another's wife, and enmity without cause. She called the third the worst. Do you agree — that hurting someone without cause is worse even than lying? And does the heart really change the moment a weapon comes into the hand — as fire flares the moment it is fed with wood?

3 · The Tale of the Sword · · THE TALE OF THE SWORD

Sita said — "Rama, let me tell you an old tale. Long ago, in a dense forest like this one, there lived a holy ascetic."

"He was a very righteous sage. Day and night he practised tapas, and his heart was calm and pure. Even the animals and birds of the forest were not afraid of him — they would come and sit beside him."

"One day Indra — the king of the gods — came there in the guise of a warrior. In his hand was a terrible sword. He said to the ascetic — 'O sage, this sword cannot stay with me. Please keep it with you — and return it when I ask for it.'"

"The ascetic took the sword — and kept it beside him."

Sita said: "Rama, it was right there that everything went wrong. The sword was always beside him — sleeping and waking, walking and sitting, even while he meditated. And slowly, the company of the sword changed his heart."

"The ascetic who was once calm became angry. The one who was once kind became harsh. With the sword always in his hand, he did violent deeds — and in the end he went to hell."

Sita looked at Rama and said — "Rama, the company of a weapon is like the company of fire — stay close, and there is always the fear of burning. I am afraid that the same may happen to you — bow in hand, vowed to kill the rakshasas — as happened to that ascetic."

Pause and think — The ascetic had done nothing wrong — he had only kept a sword beside him. And yet the company of the sword changed his heart. Can a thing change our hearts — even without being used? And is the company of a weapon really like the company of fire?

4 · Sita's Plea · · SITA'S PLEA

Sita went on — "Rama, I am not saying you should never fight the rakshasas. I am saying — killing one who has done no wrong is not right. Even if he is a rakshasa — until he commits an offence, killing him is not right."

Sita said: "A kshatriya's bow in the forest is for one thing only — to protect those who suffer. To protect the afflicted — that is the dharma of the bow. Not to kill without cause."

"And Rama, look — we have taken on the garb of ascetics. We are living in the forest as ascetics live. The dharma of an ascetic is non-violence, peace, and purity of heart. Bearing arms goes against the ascetic's garb."

"When we return to Ayodhya, then practise your kshatriya dharma — there it will be your dharma. But in this forest, in this garb — bearing arms is not right."

At last Sita said — "Rama, only my weakness makes me speak like this. Otherwise — what could I teach about dharma to you, who are the very form of dharma? Take counsel with Lakshmana too — and do what you think is good."

And Sita fell silent. Peace returned to the forest — only the rustling of leaves and the sound of birds far away.

Pause and think — Sita said — I have not come to teach you dharma, only to tell you my worry. And at the end she said — take counsel with Lakshmana too. Is taking counsel a weakness — or wisdom? And can a person — however great — stop and listen to his wife's worry?

5 · Rama's Reply — The Sages' Cry · · RAMA'S REPLY — THE SAGES' CRY

Rama listened to Sita's words — all of them, without interrupting once. Then he said slowly — "Sita, your worry is right. But now hear my words too."

"Sita, the sages of the Dandaka forest came to me themselves — I did not call them. They came to me of their own accord, and asked me for shelter."

Rama said: "Those sages live in the forest eating roots and fruits. They live in the forest at all times — but they find no peace. Fierce, flesh-eating rakshasas eat them and torment them."

"When the time of the homa comes — when they pour offerings into the fire — the rakshasas come and torment them. On festival days too — on full-moon and new-moon days — they come and disturb the sacrifice."

"Sita, those sages could destroy the rakshasas by the power of their tapas — but they do not. For their tapas was earned by long years of labour — and they do not wish to lose it. So they came to me — and said — 'Rama, you alone are our refuge, protect us.'"

(Raise your voice a little here — Rama is telling of the sages' suffering.)

"I asked them — 'What shall I do?' Then all of them together said one thing — 'Rama, there are many rakshasas in the Dandaka forest, who change their form at will. They torment us greatly. Protect us.'"

Pause and think — The sages could have destroyed the rakshasas by their tapas — but they did not, because they did not wish to lose their tapas. Was that weakness — or wisdom? And when someone asks you for protection, do you give your word — however hard it may be?

6 · Rama's Reply — The Vow · · RAMA'S REPLY — THE VOW

Rama went on — "Sita, I have given those sages my word — that I will protect them. And having given my word, I cannot break it."

Rama said: "Sita, truth is dearer to me than life itself. I would give up my life — I would give up you — I would give up Lakshmana — but I will not break the promise I made to the brahmanas."

Rama's voice was calm — but there was an unshakable firmness in it. Sita looked at him — and understood that Rama's word was no ordinary thing.

"Sita, what you said — you said it with love, and you said it rightly. Killing one who has done no wrong is not right — I know that too. But these rakshasas are offenders — they eat the sages, they disturb their sacrifices. Protecting the sages is my dharma — and my vow as well."

"And Sita — my bow will rise only against those who torment the sages. Not to kill anyone without cause."

Sita heard Rama's words — and her heart grew calm. She said nothing — she only looked at Rama, and slowly nodded.

Pause and think — Rama said — I would give up my life, give up you, give up Lakshmana — but I will not break my word. Is a promise really greater than life itself? And did Rama call Sita's worry wrong — or did he hear it, and then speak his own words? Is listening to someone's worry itself a way of honouring them?

7 · The Road Ahead · · THE ROAD AHEAD

The conversation ended. The three set out again — Rama ahead, Sita in the middle, Lakshmana behind.

The forest was still the same — tall trees, deep shade, the sound of birds. But in the hearts of the three, one thing was now clear — Rama has given his word, and he will keep it.

Sita had spoken her worry — and Rama had given his answer. Each had listened to the other — and that is the greatest thing in this story.

Ahead, the road led toward the hermitage of the sage Agastya — where Rama was to receive divine weapons, and from where the road to Panchavati would open.

Pause and think — Sita spoke her worry — and Rama gave his answer. Each listened to the other. Is that how a conversation ends — one wins and the other loses? Or does a conversation end like this — each understanding the other? And can you too speak your worry to the one you love — as Sita did?

Bigger Thoughts · · BIGGER THOUGHTS

There is no battle in this story — only a conversation. Yet this conversation is one of the deepest in the whole Ramayana.

Sita asked Rama — is killing without enmity dharma? Rama answered — having given my word, keeping it is dharma. Both were right — and each listened to the other.

Ask the listeners:

1. Sita counted three evils — falsehood, coveting another's wife, and enmity without cause. She called the third the worst. Do you agree?

2. In the sword story the ascetic did nothing wrong — he only kept a sword beside him. And yet his heart changed. Can a thing change our hearts — even without being used?

3. Sita said — a kshatriya's bow in the forest is only for protecting those who suffer. Should a weapon's work be only protection — or is attack ever right?

4. The sages could have destroyed the rakshasas by their tapas — but they did not, because they did not wish to lose their tapas. Was that weakness — or wisdom?

5. Rama said — I would give up my life, give up you, give up Lakshmana — but I will not break my word. Is a promise really greater than life itself?

6. Sita spoke her worry — and Rama heard it, without interrupting once. Is listening to someone's worry itself a way of honouring them?

7. In this story no one wins and no one loses — each understood the other. Should a conversation end like that?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main source

The main story of this book is from Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda, sargas 9–10 — Sita's question to Rama as they walk after leaving Sutikshna, and Rama's reply.

The three evils — Sarga 9

The three evils born of desire — speaking falsehood, coveting another man's wife, and enmity without cause — and the third being the worst of the three — are in sarga 9. The image of the kshatriya's heart flaring like fire fed with wood when a bow comes into his hand is also from sarga 9.

The tale of the sword — Sarga 9

The holy ascetic in the forest, Indra coming in the guise of a warrior and leaving a sword with him for safekeeping, the ascetic's heart changing through the sword's company, his growing cruel and going to hell — this is the tale Sita tells in sarga 9.

Sita's plea — Sarga 9

Sita saying that she speaks out of love and respect, not to teach him dharma; that a kshatriya's bow in the forest is only for protecting the suffering; that bearing arms goes against the ascetic's garb; that on returning to Ayodhya Rama may practise kshatriya dharma; and that he should take counsel with Lakshmana — all this is in sarga 9.

The sages' cry — Sarga 10

The sages of the Dandaka forest coming to Rama themselves to beg for shelter, living on roots and fruits, being eaten by flesh-eating rakshasas, tormented at the times of homa and festivals, able to destroy the rakshasas by their tapas yet unwilling to lose their tapas, and saying — "you alone are our refuge" — is in sarga 10.

Rama's vow — Sarga 10

Rama saying that having given his word he cannot break it; that he would give up his life, give up Sita, give up Lakshmana — but not break the promise made to the brahmanas; that truth is dearer to him than life — is in sarga 10.

What happens next

After this conversation the three walk on toward the hermitage of the sage Agastya — that story is in the next book of this series.

The End · · THE END

Here the story of Sita's worry rests — a wife's question, a husband's answer, and a vow that leads Rama toward battle with the rakshasas of the Dandaka forest.

And whenever a worry rises in your own heart, remember Sita — who spoke her words with love, with respect, and without fear. And whenever someone speaks their worry to you, remember Rama — who heard the whole of it, without interrupting once.

‖ The End ‖
